questions.question: What does it mean that WOTS is a one-time signature scheme?
options: A single secret key must be used to sign at most one message.
A signature can be verified only once.
A key pair expires after one day.
The signer must delete the public key after signing.
questions.explanation: Security relies on not leaking multiple intermediate chain values from the same private key; reuse breaks the assumptions.

questions.question: If you know an intermediate hash-chain value H^a(x), what can you compute easily (without inverting H)?
options: x
A collision in H
questions.explanation: Hash chains are forward-computable: you can apply H more times, but you can't go backwards without breaking preimage resistance.

questions.question: Why does WOTS represent the message digest in base w?
options: To trade off signature size (number of chains) against hash work (chain lengths).
Because SHA-256 only outputs base-w digits.
To make signatures independent of the hash function output length.
So that signatures can be verified without knowing w.
questions.explanation: Larger w means fewer chains (shorter signatures) but more hashing per chain; base-w digits make that trade-off explicit.

questions.question: With n = 32 bytes and w = 16, what is len_1 in RFC 8391 parameter derivation?
In this lesson's implementation, if sig[i] = H^{d_i}(sk[i]) and pk[i] = H^{w-1}(sk[i]), how does a verifier derive pk[i] from sig[i]?
options: Hash sig[i] exactly (w - 1 - d_i) times.
Hash sig[i] exactly d_i times.
Invert H on sig[i] exactly d_i times.
XOR sig[i] with the message digit d_i.
questions.explanation: Verification completes the chain: H^{w-1-d_i}(H^{d_i}(sk[i])) = H^{w-1}(sk[i]).

questions.question: What is the checksum in WOTS primarily preventing?
options: Forging a new message by only increasing some message digits (hashing forward) without needing any preimages.
Hash collisions in SHA-256.
Side-channel leakage of timing information.
Public-key substitution attacks.
questions.explanation: Without a checksum, a signature can often be transformed into signatures for 'larger' digit vectors by hashing forward; checksum digits force a decrease somewhere.

questions.question: What does WOTS+ add compared to 'plain' WOTS (high level)?
options: Per-step domain separation and masking so each hash invocation is randomized by an address/seed.
It makes the scheme safe for unlimited signatures with the same key.
It replaces hash chains with RSA exponentiation.
It removes the need for a checksum.
questions.explanation: WOTS+ keeps the one-time nature but strengthens the chaining function with address-based tweaks/masks to avoid structural issues.

questions.question: What is the most important operational rule when using WOTS inside a larger scheme like XMSS?
options: Never reuse the same WOTS private key elements (chain starts) to sign two different messages.
Always choose w as large as possible.
Always publish signatures before public keys.
Always truncate SHA-256 to 16 bytes.
questions.explanation: XMSS manages many one-time keys with a Merkle tree; breaking the 'one-time' rule breaks the security story.
